utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Thursday, the 28th of February, 2008. Good morning to the Prosecution. Good morning, Mr. Theunens, our expert witness. Good morning, Mr. Seselj, and good morning to everyone assisting us in this courtroom. Let me give you some information. We need to complete the testimony of Mr. Theunens today. Mr. Seselj has one hour and 12 minutes left. In other words, if there is no delay because of procedural matters, we should or we could be able to complete the cross-examination before the first break. There might be some re-examination, I don't know, but Mr. Marcussen, yes, is indicating that it's quite likely. In any case, after the break, we'll resume the hearing, but then a technical matter will arise, because the following witness is a protected witness, and we'll need another break to take the necessary arrangements. In any case, we'll have to stop at 12.00, because at 12.00 I have to attend the plenary, the Judges' plenary. Three amendments to the Rules are on the agenda of the plenary, so I should attend the plenary, as well as my fellow judge, Judge Harhoff. We'll stop around 12:00, and we'll resume in this case on next Tuesday. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: A very brief point in relation to the translation issue that came up yesterday. This was an issue of whether, in Exhibit number 1814 -- 1841, sorry, the words "zvanje" in B/C/S should be translated as "rank" or "title" or what the correct translation was. We received a message from CLSS. Rather than clarifying the transcript, they have sent us a message clarifying their view on the translation of this particular exhibit. The message reads: "According to the main bilingual Serbian-English dictionary, the word 'zvanje' can be translated as 'title,''rank,''profession,''calling,' 'vocation.' In the context, we would favour the word 'title'. An amended translation is attached." What I propose to do is, with leave of the Court, to change the e-court and give to Your Honours and the accused a revised translation of the document where the word "rank" is replaced with "title"; but as the document is admitted, I can obviously not tamper with what is already admitted on record without permission of Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. CLSS seems to be confirming Mr. Seselj's version. It should be translated by "title," then. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have copies here we can distribute. As Your Honours have also received hard copies, maybe everyone should have a copy.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that explanation is not complete. The interpreters working here are people with very limited -- a limited general knowledge level and they can't understand many things. They would have to be more proficient in military terminology. In military terminology, "rank," in military Yugoslav terminology, "rank" and "title" could never be synonyms. "Zvanje" can sometimes be for rank but not military rank. You can have the calling of a clergyman, for example, zvanje in the calling of a clergyman, and then you can say the bishop led the liturgy in his capacity of zvanje. But when it comes to restricted military service, then rank and title, zvanje, can never be synonyms and any Serbian military expert will confirm that. Now those translators of yours don't seem to have any general education, quite obviously, and then they make these extremely big and significant mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what I understand from the memo read out by Mr. Marcussen, CLSS used several dictionaries to look into the matter, and they believe that the word as it is used in the Serbian language may be translated by "title," but may, in some cases, be translated by the word "rank," and so on and so forth. However, CLSS concluded that the most appropriate translation would be "title." That's why Mr. Marcussen is proposing that we should replace "rank" by "title." We've taken due note of what you've stated, as you can see. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this explanation, given in that way, follows the ambitions of the Prosecution, because the Prosecution would like to have it presented -- well, it wasn't a mistake. The "rank" was used instead of "title," but what they're saying is, "In future, we're not going to use 'rank' as a synonym for 'zvanje,' 'title'." I insist that in military terminology, "cin" [phoen] meaning rank and "zvanje" meaning title could never have been synonyms, and the explanation given by your translators is unacceptable. They're not sufficiently professional to provide that type of explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you've said is now in the transcript. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, sorry, I don't think I need to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. After considering the matter, the Trial Chamber has decided that in the transcript, the English word "rank" should be translated -- should be replaced by the word "title." Whenever something is translated by "rank," it should be replaced by "title." Before giving the floor to Mr. Seselj, I have a question to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the next few days, the trial of Mr. Simatovic and Stanisic will start. They are mentioned in the indictment as part of the joint criminal enterprise. I would like to know whether you worked in the Simatovic and Stanisic case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and I was also, in that case, asked by the Prosecution to compile a report on -- in that -- for that case on the participation of forces of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia in the conflict in Croatia, 1991-1992, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1992-1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I just wanted you to confirm this for me. Mr. Seselj, you have one hour and 12 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you ride your bike yesterday?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I'm very pleased that in The Hague, I can commute by bicycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why don't you answer my question. Were you on your bike yesterday, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The witness did answer the question. He said, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the answer is, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpretation I got was not an affirmative answer. In the interpretation, all I heard was that the witness was pleased that in The Hague, he could commute by bicycle, not that he rode his bicycle yesterday. And I'm telling you, your interpreters are not doing their job properly. I've just received the affirmative answer now by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Theunens, while you were riding your bike yesterday, did anybody draw your attention to the fact that what I put to you yesterday was true, the fact I put to you yesterday, that General Aleksandar Vasiljevic was appointed as -- was named in the indictment against Slobodan Milosevic as a member of the inner circle of the joint criminal enterprise, whereas his name does not appear in my indictment as a participant in the joint criminal enterprise. Did anybody confirm to you the truthfulness of that fact?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm confused by the question, because this is the first time in my recollection this question is put to me, so I don't understand the link with anybody -- of communicating with me while I'm riding on the bicycle on that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj is a man of great wit, and he wants to know whether you can confirm that Mr. Vasiljevic was at first mentioned in the indictment, but then was not mentioned in his own indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I remember that Aleksandar Vasiljevic was mentioned in the Milosevic indictment, but I'm not 100 per cent certain about the members of the alleged JCE that are identified in the indictment against Mr. Seselj, because that's outside my sphere of competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As these professional services of the Tribunal are capacitated in order to be handled -- to be able to handle electronic devices, I don't suppose that it's a problem for them to present that portion of the Milosevic indictment on our screens. Mr. President, with your permission, I'd like to make a comment about the question earlier on and your reactions. I did not intend to be witty at all. I am quite convinced that in these proceedings, a new professional term has come into being, which in future will be customary in legal terminology, it would appear, and that in future, in other similar trials, the term "riding a bike" will be used -- the phrase "riding a bike" will be used to denote subsequent influence exerted on the witness during the break, which is absolutely prohibited. So that was the sense of my question. But if we're not able to have this portion of the indictment against Milosevic up on our screens, let me tell you that it was the Croatian and Bosnian indictment, so-called. I'd like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, how many times did you encounter -- you don't have the right to comment when I address the Trial Chamber. I'm just beginning to ask you my question now and address you. How many times, Mr. Theunens, did you meet General Aleksandar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would still like to address the comment made by Mr. Seselj, because I see it as an attack on my credibility. Since I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please prevent that, Judge. He does not have the right to comment on my addressing the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. The question seemed to be totally irrelevant to me, and I thought that Mr. Seselj was being witty. And whether he was asking if whilst riding your bicycle you suddenly remembered that Mr. Vasiljevic was mentioned in the indictment, but then Mr. Seselj added something more. He seemed to imply that somebody yesterday may have tried to influence you, and this I find extremely disturbing. That's why I would like to ask you the following: When you left this Tribunal, whilst you were riding your bicycle, even, did somebody call you to tell you, "Hey, be careful about this General Vasiljevic matter"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, since I started my testimony on the 13th of February, nobody from the OTP, nor from any other organisation, has contacted me to address issues related to my testimony, and I think it's very important to emphasise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, fine. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked the question. I asked Mr. Theunens how many times he met General Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I met General Vasiljevic when he was interviewed as a suspect in Belgrade. Now, I'm not sure whether that was in 2002 or 2003. And then I also met General Vasiljevic in The Hague during his proofing for his testimony in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Theunens, why I was never provided with a transcript of the interview of General Vasiljevic as a suspect, although during that questioning he mentioned my name and the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, such matters are obviously outside of my competence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you will recall, I'm sure, your instructions that I be provided with all the confidential -- or, rather, all the material that the Prosecution has in its possession which could be relevant to my defence in any sense, and you have another document here in addition to the questioning of General Panic and the interview of General Vasiljevic in the capacity of a suspect that I have not been informed about at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. We'll now turn to the OTP in regard to this. Apparently, and it's new to me, apparently the witness took part in the proofing of General Vasiljevic. He was there also during the proofing of General Vasiljevic who apparently was heard as a suspect, and apparently the transcript was not disclosed to the accused because, according to the accused, there could be exculpatory elements in that transcript. Mr. Marcussen, can you answer this or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The only thing I can answer right now is that the accused has received, in B/C/S, the transcript of the Milosevic hearings, and he would therefore have received the B/C/S version of General Vasiljevic's testimony in the Milosevic case. I would need a little bit of time to find out what material relating to General Vasiljevic had been disclosed to the accused, so I cannot answer that right now. And, as usual, I'd like to make sure that we get you the right information on this. I think the accused said that he had a right to receive this because there had been an order that anything that mentions General -- sorry, anything that mentions his name should be given to him, and as I said, we will have to look into it. But I'm not sure that he is saying that he needs to get this because the material is exculpatory. And from what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, one follow-up question. General Vasiljevic testified in the Milosevic case. He probably made a written statement, a signed statement, and this statement, I suppose, must have been disclosed to Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj was probably given both the written statement and the transcript of the testimony. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, we are checking the records a bit on the fly. What I can say is that on the 28th of January, 2005, the accused was provided a CD with the suspect interview on it, which he refused. I'd like -- maybe if you will allow me maybe after the next break to inform you about the status of whether or not there exists a transcription of this particular interview or whether we have the same situation as we have with the Panic interview, that the OTP has not transcribed this particular suspect interview, and we will also try to look into the issue of whether or not there exists a statement. But as I said, there have definitely been attempts to disclose this material to the accused in electronic form. If we have the transcripts, I'll be able to get back to you, but I'll need a little more time to find out about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I can identify what's at stake here. It so happens that I was a member of the Pre-Trial Chamber presided by Judge Agius, and then after a number of developments I became the Pre-Trial Judge in this case. There was, indeed, a major problem in this case. The accused did not want to have a standby counsel, and he refused to accept any CD. He refused all CDs. And when I started working on this case, a number of decisions were made, asking the Prosecution to disclose in hard copy what was to be disclosed to the accused, including everything related to Rule 68(A)(i). It was also stated that the accused was authorised to provide key words to the Prosecution to make a search in the 207.000 pages, because he had been told that these 207.000 pages may be exculpatory evidence. That's the situation. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just as the issue was with Panic, if the situation is that we only have the audio version of -- audio or video version of the suspect interview, then these sort of things would not be included in the 207.000 pages or this big volume of pages that we are talking about. But after the break, I will -- I hope I'm able to bring some more clarity over what written material exists.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Marcussen has presented an untruth. He said that I was provided with the entire transcript of the testimony of General Aleksandar Vasiljevic in the Slobodan Milosevic trial. That's not true. The OTP provides me successively with transcripts of testimonies of only those people whom they plan to call in this trial as Prosecution witnesses, and as far as things stand now, the OTP does not plan to bring in General Aleksandar Vasiljevic as a witness in this trial. Everything they have provided me with and where there are portions of General Aleksandar Vasiljevic's testimony are books which were published by Natasa Kandic in her fund for humanitarian law, or whatever it's called, and they're books which contain just the public parts of the interview of the Prosecution witness in the Slobodan Milosevic trial, and General Vasiljevic testified in part in open session and in part in private sessions, secretly. I read what was stated in public, in open session, but it was only in several -- on several occasions that he asked to move into private session. So the information provided to you by Mr. Marcussen is quite obviously not true, and I can continue if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the books that the accused is referring to is reproducing it in transcript form the material that's included in the book by the Humanitarian Law Centre, and that has been a practical way of getting all this material transcribed to the accused. Mr. Vasiljevic is not on the Prosecution witness list in this case. If the accused has an interest in receiving closed session material relating to this witness, in particular, he is at liberty to make an application to the Tribunal for access to the closed session part of the testimony, and he -- the competent Judges will decide on this. This is not a disclosure problem that arises from anything the Office of the Prosecutor had done. Now, secondly, the Prosecution has made an effort to disclose all of this material to the accused. It is the accused who refuses to review, either himself or with his -- I don't remember if it's 28 or 26 assistants that he lists on all his filing. He's refusing to make use of the material that's being given to him in order to prepare his defence. If this particular issue had been something he seriously was concerned about for the cross-examination of this witness, he would have had ample time to raise this issue before today so we could have dealt with it, rather than spending the Court's time on issues like this that could have been dealt with before. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we've already spent 25 minutes on procedural matters. Mr. Marcussen is absolutely right, and that's exactly what I had in mind when he started to speak. How come your own expert, General Delic, who prepared this report for you, how come he didn't notify you a long time ago that it was essential for you to get all the material related to that particular general because he was in charge of the 1st Military District, and why didn't you say to your expert then, "We don't have the documents," and then you would have seen that it was absolutely essential to ask the Prosecution for these documents. That's what you should have done, instead of waiting the very end of the cross-examination to say that you don't have this document. You could have received this document a long time ago if you had made the proper application. All this would not have happened if the Rules had provided that disclosure is monitored by the Pre-Trial Judge, because if the Rule was organised that way, then the Pre-Trial Judge would have realised how important the role of the general was and that all material pertaining to this general should be disclosed to the accused. But since my predecessors decided that disclosure should not come under any type of monitoring or control, well, we are faced with that type of issues and problems, and we are wasting a great deal of time, time that could have been more profitably spent on the cross-examination or on the review of documents. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor. The Prosecution is telling us that they'll answer later on, and as in the case of General Panic, they say that they will disclose everything in writing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I'm surprised by this observation of yours. General Bozidar Delic was not indispensable for me to realise that I needed to use the entire testimony of General Zivota Panic, or rather his entire suspect interview. But yesterday or the day before, I told you that on the 4th of October, 2004, at the status conference that was held then, I asked for the entire transcripts of the interview with General Zivota Panic. The court administration can check this immediately and by the break they can tell you whether what I'm saying is correct. That was the first time I requested this. After that, I'm sure I requested it at least two or three times and even mentioned it in some written submissions, but there's no need for me to search for that now because I have reliable information that I did ask for it on the 4th of October, 2000, at the status conference held then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 2004, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, Mr. Marcussen says that if I feel I need the transcripts of closed session testimony from the Milosevic case, I should apply to the Court. But why should I apply to the Court when I have no information indicating that in that closed session in the Milosevic case, General Vasiljevic mentioned my name or the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party? I don't have that information, but I'm sure that he spoke about this in his suspect interview. And today, for the first time, we have heard that he actually was interviewed as a suspect and then he was not indicted. Instead of that, he's being used to do certain jobs in the OTP, to testify against Milosevic, and now we'll see how the OTP used him in the case against me. By your leave, I'd like to continue with my cross-examination. I have the least reason to waste time. You can see that I don't like taking the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you may proceed. Just a comment I'd like to make. General Vasiljevic could be an important witness. The Prosecution could have called this person to testify. The Prosecution is entitled to call the witnesses it wishes to call to testify. When the time comes for the presentation of your case, nothing prevents you from asking this witness to come. You can start off with non-leading questions, but if he appears to be hostile, in that case you can put questions to him which could be leading questions. In that case, this would be part of your cross-examination. So this is a possibility you have, even if, unfortunately, it seems that there are a number of documents which have not been disclosed to you. It is not too late. A trial starts at a particular point and ends at a particular point. We haven't reached that end point yet, and you have plenty of time to address a number of topics relating to your case; i.e., the role played by General Vasiljevic, amongst others. So you have the floor now. You have an hour and 12 minutes left for the remainder of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I call General Vasiljevic in the Defence case, I will have to apply for a subpoena, because there's no other way I can get to General Vasiljevic, but that doesn't matter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in your report you included an exhibit, 1913, and a piece of information. I will not talk about it because it's being treated as a confidential document still. But the Prosecution has confirmed that it obtained that document from General Vasiljevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be helpful if we could see the document, just to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's the unsigned document, without a date, without a stamp, without a heading, and the number is 1913.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I thank Mr. Seselj for the clarification. I believe now that I remember about which document we are talking. And I knew that the document had been provided by a sensitive source, but if the Prosecution confirms it, the sensitive source is Mr. Vasiljevic, then I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: While writing your expert report, you did not know about the source of this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I said, I knew that the document had been provided by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Marcussen, the Registrar is asking me, as far as this document is concerned, which comes from a sensitive source, whether you would like part of the transcript to be redacted or do you feel that this is pointless now, it doesn't matter if everything is in the public domain now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think General Vasiljevic has -- I think it's fine for this particular document. There has been so much talk about this now that we can leave it on the public record. I would respectfully request the accused, in future, when he gets to these kind of issues, to make sure that we avoid revealing sources, and when discussing who else had been giving evidence to the Prosecution, that we do this in private session. I think General Vasiljevic, if I can put it in these terms, is strong enough to put up with this, so let's just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, when you address this kind of issue in the future, please let us know beforehand. Let us know what kind of topic you wish to address so that we can move into private session. Nothing prevents us from going into open session after that, but we have to abide by the procedure in these matters. I'll give you the floor back now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think the OTP treated only the contents of the document as confidential. If you recall from my statement at the beginning of the trial, the name of General Aleksandar Vasiljevic has not been confidential. I mentioned his name in the pre-trial phase, and Madam Christine intervened very energetically, and you said I could not use the names of potential OTP witnesses in public session. And I asked you directly whether, in my statement of the accused at the beginning of the trial, I could mention the name of General Vasiljevic, who was the chief of security of the JNA. This is just a summary. It's not what was said literally. And you said, "Well, of course, you can, because he was a public figure. He was a high-ranking officer," and this was all in late October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did not know at the time that General Vasiljevic had been heard as a suspect. I didn't know that his name was mentioned in the indictment. I didn't know at the time that he then was no longer prosecuted. I didn't know some of the information relating to him. So if he was a general in the JNA, then there's no reason why a document provided by the JNA be kept confidential. However, the sensitive issues here have just come to light. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think you have been perfectly clear on this, and we really shouldn't be spending time on this. It's got to be clear to the accused as well. The issue is revealing the source of material given to the Court, in this instance through the Office of the Prosecutor. That is the concern. Of course, General Vasiljevic is known, he has been discussed in open court. This is not the issue. The issue is the source of information provided, and that's what has to be in closed session -- in private session, ought to have been, but the cat is out of the bag and that's fine. But I hope the accused would acknowledge this distinction and respect Your Honour's decision on this in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I must read out Article 70(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence which has to do with exceptions to the rules of disclosure. If some material has been disclosed confidentially, and if this information has only been provided in order to provide new evidence, the Prosecution cannot provide this initial material, and the source of the material without the consent of the person having providing it or the body having provided it. These sources can never be used as evidence before having been disclosed to the Prosecution. So the Rule has provided for the situation in which the Prosecution has in its possession very confidential information provided by state or a private individual, and this material cannot be disclosed -- and can only be disclosed if the source agrees. This is what the Rules of Procedure says regarding this particular matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, by your leave, that provision of the Rules does not pertain to this case at all, because as you can see, this is a document which is an exhibit, and it was provided in these three binders as material tendered in the course of the testimony of the expert witness of the OTP. When the Prosecutor tried to tender this document in the course of the examination-in-chief, I objected because the document has no identifying markings, and the Prosecutor couldn't say anything about this. I expressed my doubts, based on the style of writing. That's why I thought it had been done by General Vasiljevic. And on the following day, the Prosecutor confirmed that he really had done this. I am just reminding you of what happened in the course of the past few days, and you have all been eyewitnesses to this. This is not a document giving certain information to the OTP which they are using to search for other documents rather than using it as an exhibit. They did try to tender this document as an exhibit unsuccessfully. And also it's a document quoted by this expert in his expert report, so this document is being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid making a mistake, could you just tell me whether I can now speak in public session about the contents of the document or should I not mention them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may now talk about this document in open session without any problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, please correct these sources can never be used as evidence before having been disclosed to the accused and not the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The following: When this document came into your hands, probably from the OTP archives, did you ask yourself whether you should check who the author of the document was, when it was compiled, to whom it was addressed, and its other identifying features, before you used it in the writing of your expert report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, I did so, and I think it's helpful in this context to make the distinction between the source and the provider. The source of the document, i.e., the person or the organisation that drafted the document, can be -- even though it is not clearly indicated or explicitly indicated in the document, can be derived from the first paragraph of the document, when you see under the title it is written: "In working of the counter-intelligence protection of the Armed Forces, VJ security organs ..." And so on and so on. Now, obviously I read also through the article itself. Now, to explain the provider, each document that is -- that becomes available to the Office of the Prosecutor is recorded in a database and can be -- the information pertaining to when it was obtained, from whom it was obtained, how it was obtained, as well as a short summary of the document is stored and can be consulted. And obviously I consulted that information for all the documents I included in the report, as it is part of the methodology I applied when compiling this report, and so I could see in the database that the document had been provided, which is not the same as the source, it had been provided by a sensitive source, which has been discussed extensively here. I would also like to draw the Court's attention to the fact that I only used this document to explain that according to that document, volunteer groups had received weapons, small arms, from depots of the former JNA, MUP, and the Serbian Ministry of Defence, and that these weapons were distributed before these volunteers went to the battlefields or the crisis areas in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, this is in part 2 of the report. In part 3 of the report, when discussing the arming and equipment of SRS volunteers, we can actually see that the information included in this security organ or Security Administration report is actually corroborated by documents of the SRS war staff or statements of members of the SRS war staff and also statements of Mr. Seselj himself, so I find it hard to understand that there is such a problem being made about including this document in my report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to draw your attention again to the fact that this was not an answer to my question, but you continue to tolerate these expansive replies which do not contain an answer to my question and yet waste my valuable time. But there's nothing I can do about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand your concern. Now you're putting the question. You want to know whether, in the course of his work, he pinpointed the origin of the document, and he said, "Yes," because they have a database that enables him to conduct this kind of research. Notwithstanding the sensitive nature of this document, he felt this document could be mentioned in his report because this document related to the arming of the volunteers, and so on and so forth. He has answered the question. Now, maybe you might not like his answer, which I fully understand, but if you don't like his answer, you can continue putting to him questions on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, what does this number 194 mean, the handwritten figure at the top of the first page?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a number given -- that can be given by the person who compiled the document or the person who provided the document. I have not been able to establish that. And it's probably a registration number, but I cannot provide additional information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What does this date mean, the 19th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date may refer to the date that the document was finalised or was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the document -- and you can see that from the text, do you agree, because from the text, it's evident that there was a big clash ongoing between the Serbian Radical Party and the regime, which arose in September, when we demanded that the government of Serbia be toppled? This was in mid-September of 1993. Do you know of this? Please answer briefly. If you don't know, we'll move on right away.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am familiar, in general terms, with the political conflict that arose in the, yeah, September, November 1993 time period between Mr. Seselj and Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In what capacity did the General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, on the 19th of October, 1993, or in what capacity could he have written this document? Tell me that, as a military expert.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document does not state that it was -- that it was written or compiled by Mr. Vasiljevic. That is what I have tried to explain earlier, to make a distinction between the source, i.e., the person or the organisation signing a document, or -- and when it's not signed, well, you try to derive from the contents of the document, and I drew the attention on the first paragraph. So the source does not have to be the same person or organisation as the provider. The document does not allow to identify who -- I mean, Mr. X, Y or Z -- drafted the document. The document only allows to conclude that it was compiled by security organs of the VJ. So when we talk about the VJ, so it has to be -- it must have been compiled after May 1992, when the VJ replaced the JNA. That's all we can say. Mr. Theunens, as a military expert, could you explain, how come on the first day I recognised that the author of this document was General Vasiljevic by the style of writing? How could I have done that? Do I have some sort of supernatural powers or am I simply familiar with General Vasiljevic's style of writing? How could I have drawn that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is not a question that the witness can answer. It calls for pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the witness cannot answer this kind of question, and the style of writing of the general is something perhaps he's not familiar with. So, Mr. Theunens, do you have an answer for this question or don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say it's a claim Mr. Seselj makes, but it would be -- it would have to be verified if we really want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To cut it short, in this document it says that the Serbian Radical Party, in Serbia, formed paramilitary detachments. Certain municipalities are mentioned, and so on and so forth. This was a time when the Serbian Radical Party was engaged in a vehement conflict with the Milosevic regime. In your report, you state that this was a period of large-scale arrests of members of the Serbian Radical Party and especially its volunteers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document talks -- addresses events in 1991 and 1992, in particular in the context of the arming of paramilitary groups, arming by Ministry of Interior and JNA. The listing of paramilitary groups, from the document we cannot conclude whether this list of groups applies to the situation in September or October of 1993 or whether it actually is a list of organisation that existed actually in 1991 or 1992. So when looking at the document, I do not see a link between the contents of the document and the political conflict between Mr. Seselj and Mr. Milosevic from October 1993. I have indeed mentioned in my report that -- and I think I make reference to a statement by Branislav Vakic, who was a senior SRS volunteer, that after or during the political conflict between Mr. Seselj and Mr. Milosevic, a large number of SRS volunteers were arrested. From my work in the Milosevic trial, I -- and the documents I had access to at that stage, I came to the conclusion that most of these volunteers were released after having been charged, for example, for illegal possession of arms, or only received minor punishments. There were at the time no significant war crimes trials in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you aware that after our initiative to topple the government, the government of Nikola Sainovic lost its majority in the National Assembly, that Slobodan Milosevic dissolved the National Assembly and called new elections in December 1993? Are you aware of this? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of this in very general terms, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All these arrests of members of the Serbian Radical Party, did they take place in the course of the election campaign?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of a number of arrests during the election campaign, Your Honours, and as an outside observer, without having studied the matter in detail, one could draw indeed the conclusion that these were political arrests, that they were not arrested for the alleged crimes they had or the alleged crimes they had committed, but for political reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that only some of them were convicted of possession of weapons, which is not a very serious crime. Do you know that only two were convicted of possession of weapons, after so many arrests that took place? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware of the precise number, but it would be in line with what I said earlier, that it seemed that there were political considerations that were actually the dominating factor at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, had the regime had information that the Serbian Radical Party was really forming a paramilitary structure and paramilitary detachments in Serbia and setting up commands, would that have been sufficient reason for Milosevic to ban the Serbian Radical Party under the then Serbian legislation which was valid at the time? To put it more simply, if the things General Vasiljevic wrote in this document had been true, that there were paramilitary detachments of the Serbian Radical Party, would that have been sufficient reason for Milosevic to solve the problem of the radicals for good and simply ban the party?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, I would like to make reference to the letter by Colonel Eremija, which is 65 ter number 604. It also has an exhibit number, but I don't have it. And I would like to make the link with my testimony in the Milosevic trial, where Mr. Milosevic cross-examined me on this document, in particular on the paragraph where -- under heading 5, Colonel Eremija proposes that the organised disarming of paramilitary formations is undertaken and that the authorities of the Republic of Serbia must participate in the campaign. Mr. Milosevic then stated to me, "Well, you know, these were all groups from the opposition. The authorities were not involved." I then replied by making reference to Article 118 of the 1990 Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbia, which indeed states that only the state authorities are allowed to organise, plan, establish, train, equip armed formations, and that I would expect that in such a situation, the competent organs in a country, more specifically the state security as well as the military security, would keep a close eye on such groups. Well, I can only repeat this answer here. Mr. Milosevic was not only informed, I think, through the military chain of command, but also there is, for example, the Human Rights Watch letter which he sent to him and Adzic in January 1992 - I will provide you the 65 ter number - where mention is made of the paramilitary groups originating from Serbia and were participating in the fighting in Croatia. And the chief of cabinet of Mr. Milosevic even provides a reply to Human Rights Watch to confirm the reception of this report. Now, I will finalise my reply. Whether the report is entirely correct or not, that's not the issue, but if a head of state receives such a report from an NGO, the least he would have done is to investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. What you've just said, I was reading your cross-examination in the Milosevic trial this morning, and this is exactly what the transcript says in that case. Now, as far as what you have just said is concerned, Seselj's men, the volunteers, the volunteers of the SRS, these were paramilitaries or were these people who had been incorporated in the TO or in the JNA? What do you have to answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, from the strictly legal point of view, based on the legislation that existed until the summer of 1991, these were paramilitaries. However, as we discussed, between summer 1991 and December 1991, a number of decrees and orders were adopted on the level of the Republic of Serbia, the SSNO, as well as the SFRY Presidency, the 10th of December Presidency order, in order to legalise not only SRS volunteers but also other paramilitary or volunteer groups. And as I explained, as far as Croatia is concerned, most of the SRS volunteers were integrated in the TO, the local Serb TO that had been established, and/or the JNA; i.e., they were operating under the command of the JNA. The situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina is slightly more complicated, because there we seem to have -- or we have different arrangements depending on the time period and the area we are looking at, and that is what I have tried to explain in the second part of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did the authorities in Serbia ever legalise the Serbian Guard of Vuk Draskovic, the White Eagles or Yellow Wasps; did they ever come within the composition of the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm generally familiar with operations of -- that are ascribed to the Serbian Guard in the general area of Gospic, but I have not been able to look into detail to see what the command-and-control arrangements were in the area of Gospic, so in Western Croatia, whether or not the Serbian Guard was under command there of the JNA. White Eagles are mentioned in the Eremija report we discussed earlier. They seem to have been active in the wider area of Lovas or at least Eastern Slavonia. I do not have enough sufficient documentation of the Proletarian Guards Mechanised Division in order to establish what the command-and-control arrangements were in relation to the participation of White Eagles in that area. The Yellow Wasps, in Zvornik, we're talking about the takeover of Zvornik, April-May 1992. Based on the document I reviewed, obviously Zvornik was located in the zone of responsibility of the 17th Corps of the JNA. The 17 Corps was also alerted of the situation in the area, but the documentation I had access to does not indicate that the 17 Corps played -- or units of the 17 Corps played an active role in the Serb takeover of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Because the papers don't show it, then you considered that that was really how things stood. Right, Mr. Theunens. Now, Mr. Theunens, did you take part in preparing -- how can the witness interrupt me, Judge? Mr. Theunens, did you take part in the preparation of Goran Stoparic for testimony and the proofing of Goran Stoparic?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not involved in any proofing, or interview, or any other activity in relation to Goran Stoparic. I would just like to address the claim made by Mr. Seselj, where he says because the papers don't show it, then you consider that that's how things really stood. No, the methodology is different. I can only draw conclusions from documents. If there are no documents available for a particular issue, I do not draw conclusions. It's as simple as that. I cannot conclude what is not mentioned in a document, and especially when I don't have a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because it seems symptomatic to me that in this false document and in the false part of the testimony by Goran Stoparic in this court, the same nonexistent thing is mentioned, that the Serb Radical Party, in 1992 and 1993, formed paramilitary detachments in Serbia in the various municipalities, so that's why I'm asking you the question, because quite obviously you're searching for grounds, legal grounds, for criminal proceedings to be taken with respect to the Prosecution's thesis about the persecution of Croats from Vojvodina. Isn't that right, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not really understood the question, because I'm not sure which -- which false document you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, before we get into where we ended up yesterday, and also of allegations being made against various people being thieves and liars and things like that, I think we should caution the accused against, in this case, saying that one of the witnesses has given false testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please reformulate your question, because it's not quite -- it wasn't quite clear. I think I understood your question, but please put your question again, without any allegations about anybody, about false testimony or whatever, because this is not sufficient to disqualify anybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know full well, Mr. President, that all my questions are nebulous. I'm not protesting against that observation of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you, as a military expert of the OTP, do you have any knowledge whatsoever to the effect that during 1992 and 1993, there was any kind of attack against the Croatia civilian population in Vojvodina, in any locality?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the activities in Vojvodina are outside my scope, so I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, a few minutes ago Mr. Seselj wanted to ask a question, and you were not in a position to answer. Now he's moving forward, but the question he meant to ask seems essential to me, so I'm going to put it to you. To your knowledge, and based on the documents you reviewed, are you in a position to say that there were paramilitary units in 1992 and 1993 in Croatia, paramilitary units of the Serbian Radical Party? I want to be specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe it was a mistake in the transcript, but the question by the accused was whether there were any such activities in Vojvodina, and the expert -- Vojvodina is in Serbia. So -- no, it's just that the transcript says "Croatia"" in your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question related to Croatia first before we move on to anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the section Croatia, excuse me, Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem, I think I included, again, it's an unsigned and undated document apparently compiled by the security organ on the role of Jovo Ostojic in Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem and more specifically his activities against the local Serb population. Jovo Ostojic, who is known as being in charge of an SRS volunteer group in Sarajevo in 1992, according to SRS documentation or articles in "Velika Serbia," he was also involved in training SRS volunteers in a training camp in Pribisevica in Serbia. The Ostojic document I'm referring to is 65 ter number 4144, discussed on page 122 and 123 of my report. For Bosnia-Herzegovina, allow me to just give you one example. This is on page 203, English page 203 of part 2 of the report, where I address the participation of SRS/SCP volunteers in the Serb takeover of Bosanski Samac in April 1992. And I quote there from a statement by Zoran Obradovic, chairman of the town board of the Serbian Radical Party in Kragujevac, so a city in southern in Serbia, at the occasion of the Fatherland 3rd Congress of the Serbian Radical Party. It's a speech he makes in 1994, and I'll just read out the quotation. "Obradovic states, having completed the task," which refers to previous activity of SRS volunteers, "the war staff of the Serbian Radical Party ordered it," and he's talking about the Chetnik Sumarija Detachment, "to move, with the assistance of the air force, to the area around Bosanski Samac in order to organise a Serbian uprising against the joint Ustasha," and then it uses the term "balija," which is translated as a derogatory term for BH Muslims, "authorities." And so on and so on. This is just one example of an SRS volunteer detachment which has been formed in Serbia. It is still in existence in April 1992, and then it acts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Bosanski Samac. It states with the assistance of the air force. I drew a conclusion from that this was with the assistance of the JNA, because that's the only air force I can imagine. Serbia did not have an air force at that stage, and I don't expect that the air force of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I take good note of what you just said. But you are talking about assistance of the air force, so there must have been at least orders of resubordination of this unit, whether it was paramilitary or not, because the JNA or the VRS were not going to launch the air force into an operation without any basis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. There needs to have been a plan and a preparation of the operation, because it's not just a group who goes to an airport and says, "We need a helicopter or an aeroplane." I would just like to make a small correction. The VRS was only established in May 1992, so it has to be JNA. But otherwise, indeed, we see -- and that's what I have tried to explain when addressing the various geographic areas included in both the Croatia section as well as the Bosnia-Herzegovina section of part 2 of the report, that the SRS/SCP volunteers do not act --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop here, please. What about Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours -- I'm just waiting for the transcript. Your Honours, I have not looked into Vojvodina because that was not part of my tasking. I only addressed the role in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I would like to dwell on that for a moment, Mr. Theunens. How come the indictment incorporates the alleged crimes in Vojvodina, punishable under international war law, which implies and understands that there must have been an attack somewhere against the Croatian civilian population, and an attack must be systematic or widespread, as it says, but that you must have an attack to begin with, and you, as a military expert of the OTP, are best placed, I assume, to assess whether there was an attack at all in the first place. You say you didn't deal with that, so who's going to answer my question, then, if not you, whether there was an attack or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is not a question that can be answered by the witness. There would be led evidence about these matters later on in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your question has legal -- major legal implications. The expert told us that he was not a legal expert, so there will be further evidence, and your question will perhaps be answered, Mr. Seselj. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the only military expert of the Prosecution that they have told us about. They have nobody else who could come here and interpret, from the professional expert standpoint, whether there was an attack in Vojvodina at all against the Croatian civilian population. They're going to bring in alleged victims, people who perhaps suffered during various incidents or whatever, who had an unpleasant time, but they do not intend to call on any other military expert who can confirm, on behalf of the Prosecution, that there was indeed an attack, because if there was no attack, then that part of the indictment does not hold water. You can't add 10, 12, 15 isolated incidents and say that was an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to deal into the legal aspect of the issue, but to your knowledge, even though apparently you haven't gone into the details of the issues related to Vojvodina, can you tell us whether there has been a large attack against the Croatian population of Vojvodina, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have been called here to deal with military issues, and even if I haven't studied the matter in detail, to my recollection there hasn't been a military attack, i.e., by the VJ, in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Army of Yugoslavia, I see, you said it wasn't -- right. I was a little taken aback when I heard what was being said to me first. Thank you, Mr. Theunens. You have -- you are the most valuable witness I have had here thus far, and I'm not going to ask you any more difficult questions. I'm going to ask you easy ones now. You have confirmed a key matter in my Defence. The Prosecution might attack you, but if the OTP sack you, I will find a job for you on my Defence team. Now, Mr. Theunens, I gained the impression that during the cross-examination, you went back and corrected a part of your expert report and then confirmed that, in a way, the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were involved in the war areas of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem until September 1991, and that they were engaged in a different way after September 1991. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I tried to say, I think this was in response to a question by the Prosecutor where I was asked to summarise my conclusions, it is that prior to September or indeed earlier, middle or end of September, 1991, the documents I have consulted in relation to Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem indicate that the SRS/SCP volunteers are operating without being part of a wider force which is commanded and controlled by the JNA. I mean by that that they operate in cooperation with local village defences, local Serb TO. There is no systematic involvement of the JNA in the areas where SRS/SCP volunteers are active. In the course of the month of September, and I use that date because it's -- it's -- it's linked to the appointment of General Zivota Panic as the commander of the 1st Military District, he's then appointed as the person in charge of the operations, the JNA operations in Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem, and he establishes two operational groups, OG North and OG South. And from the documentation I have consulted, we can see that SRS/SCP volunteers operate in OG South. Those that are part of the Petrova Gora and Leva Supoderica, local Serb TO detachments in Vukovar, are -- operate under the command and control of the Guards Motorised Brigade until at least the 21st of November at 6.00 in the morning. And that's actually shown in the document or the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Just please try and give me brief answers. I confirm the truthfulness of your words, that up until September 1991, the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party had no links with the JNA. Now, is it obvious to you, then, from the report by Srecko Radovanovic who writes in one section that when the JNA entered a certain village, the volunteers withdrew straightaway, they avoided any meeting with the JNA. Did you note that in his report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, but I would just like to come back to when Mr. Seselj says, "I confirm the truthfulness of your words," stating that the SRS volunteers had no links with the JNA, I mean by that that they were not operating under the command and control of the JNA in the area. Whether there were other links, I have not answered that question. And what Srecko Radovanovic states, yes, and it actually confirms also -- it corresponds with what Ljubisa Petkovic stated in another public statement, probably a "Velika Serbia" article, when he said that for what Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem is concerned, the SRS volunteers did not want to cooperate with the JNA. This was probably a statement from prior to September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, that's a very important thing here. You saw that the Serbian radical volunteers existed in many countries --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In many villages, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: ... 10 or 15 villages, in fact. And then Ljubisa Petkovic, at the beginning of September, asks that all the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party be returned to Serbia? Do you remember that piece of paper? And Zoran Rankic goes into the field to convey that to them? Do you remember those papers, to avoid looking for the documents in these files? It takes up a long time, but they've been presented here, anyway, earlier on.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the document. Then if we are talking about Eastern Slavonia, then I think it's incorrect, but it would be helpful to see the document because I'm trying to find it, whether it's in my report or not, because I don't remember the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Srecko Radovanovic mentions that at the end of his report, too, that he was ordered to withdraw volunteers who were under his command, to withdraw them to Serbia. And he describes in his report which fighting he took part in, what the results of that combat were, and finally he says that he was given the order to withdraw to Serbia. You will find that in Zoran Rankic's writings, too, in a report where he complains that a group of volunteers did not wish to withdraw to Serbia, and he mentions Trpinja and Branislav Gavrilovic-Brne, that he refused to return to Serbia. All those documents were shown here. If you can't find them, I don't have time to waste looking for them, if you can't remember and recall that. Do you agree with me? Tell me if you agree that all the volunteers were withdrawn from Slavonia to Serbia, and that from September onwards, they were sent within the composition of the JNA to units which were exclusively under the command of the JNA, and that's my thesis.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot entirely agree, because I think we're mixing different documents in different areas. So it would be helpful just to refresh my memory to see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, have you got Srecko Radovanovic's document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to see the documents, but we're going to try and deal with the most important issue. What the accused says is that starting in September 1991, the SRS asks and invites the volunteers to go back to Serbia, and that when they arrive in Serbia, they will be put under the command of the JNA. Do you agree with this idea or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To help the witness remember, I'm sure you'll recall that it was ordered that the volunteers should return in order to regroup.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer the question of the Presiding Judge, yes, I do remember that Srecko Radovanovic issued such an order to the volunteers under his command, to those volunteers, and indeed as I said earlier, that from September onwards the volunteers operating, at least those in Eastern Slavonia, so in the wider area of Vukovar, are under the command of the JNA. I just want to add one small comment. That is for Western Slavonia. That is, when there is an exchange of letters and reports between the Command of the 5th JNA Corps, General Talic, and the military prosecutor in the area, and this document is included in my report, to discuss crimes that were committed or allegedly committed in the area of Vocin around the 10th of September, Talic notifies --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What has this to do with my question? Mr. President, please, well, intervene at least once. We're talking about Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we're only talking about Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we're talking about up to September, up to the month of September, no a single volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party was in Western Slavonia, isn't that right? So don't mix things up before September and after September, if you're able to do that. Are you able to do that? So up until September, the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were defending certain villages, called in by the local Serb population to do so. Now, do you know that those volunteers crossed over into Slavonia, crossed the Danube or Srem, and they had to hide from the authorities in Serbia to do that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all I would like to comment on the fact -- on the claim made by Mr. Seselj that these volunteers had been called by the local Serb population to come to the area. I would like to refer you to English page 104 in part 2 of the report, where the activities of the Chetnik Volunteer Detachment that participated in the -- okay, the conflict in Borovo Sela on the 2nd of May is being discussed, and according to 65 ter number 320, that's Chetnik Volunteer Detachment had been established following a decision by the Central Homeland Administration of the Serbian Chetnik Movement and was then dispatched to Western Srem on the 2nd of April, 1991. Now, the circumstances of how these volunteers went from Serbia to Croatia. Indeed, articles of "Velika Serbia" suggested the volunteers did not use one of the three bridges over the Danube, but that they crossed the Danube by night using boats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you could have given a much shorter answer to that question, because that's the essence of it. If you said they went -- crossed the river in boats by night, that would have sufficed. Why go on with all the other things you said. That's what I'm saying, anyway. Now do you know how these volunteers were armed, what weapons they had and where they obtained them from?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, that these volunteers had small arms. In some cases, they received the weapons in the -- in the villages they went to, so these weapons had been provided there one way or the other. I've also seen, and that's actually included in the section on training and equipment of the SRS volunteers, that, as I said earlier, that SRS volunteers received weapons from JNA, with the assist -- and from the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and sometimes with the assistance of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I don't think the witness does not understand my questions. I think he is intentionally engaged in subversive activity of my defence and the cross-examination. I am asking him up until September 1991, exclusively up until that month, the month of September 1991. Now, he's already said they received weapons in the villages they went to. There's not single shred of evidence that they got it from the JNA and carried it in from Serbia. But my question was what type of weapons. He said infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, I would like to know specifications. If we're talking about rifles, automatic rifles, what kind of weapons? And as a military expert, you must know the kind of weapons and be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, himself, when he spoke to the Death of Yugoslavia documentary, and this is mentioned on page 42, part 2 of the report, spoke about Thompson guns, which are quite old, small machine-guns, M-48 guns or rifles, and then there's something he called a Tandzara, but I'm not familiar with that. So in summary, these are most of the time old, small arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, this Thompson gun, is it really an automatic rifle? What do you think, as an officer?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's a difficult question, isn't it? Shall I withdraw it if it's that difficult?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I will try to answer the question to my best abilities. I never operated a Thompson, but I think it has a round charger and I'm not sure whether it's entirely automatic so that it can fire all rounds in one attempt or whether it can only fire shot by shot and small bursts. But I'm familiar with the type of weapon. I think it was even used in the Second World War by the British forces, if my recollection is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are we dealing with a rifle? Is it a rifle? Just answer that, please.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you, as a military expert and an officer of the courageous Belgian Army, do you know what the difference is between an automatic and an automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please answer the question, because I must say I was quite taken aback by what you'd said before. I thought that a Thompson gun was more a machine-gun, a small machine-gun, and you're telling us it's a rifle. What's the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Between an automatic and an automatic rifle, the difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the issue has to do with the translation. When I meant "rifle," I actually meant that it's, in my view, an automatic rifle. Now, because "gun" can also be used for "cannon," so it's -- yeah, I don't have a picture here, but it looks -- in French, you could say "mitraillette," but of small calibre. Now, the question Mr. Seselj talks about, an automatic and an automatic rifle, I'm not sure what is meant by the first term. I want to make a distinction between, for example, what is known as a Thompson and then a heavy machine-gun, for example, what we have, the MAG, which is what -- or what you often see in movies, like the point 50, which is a machine-gun. Now, the Thompson is closer to a Kalashnikov, for example, when you look in very general terms at the weapons system, than to a point 50 or the MAG machine-gun, if that helps to clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's five past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a short question, if I may, Your Honour, Judge, to round off this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please finish on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what a German Schmeisser is, dating back to the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's a small, well, you call it and in French "mitraillette."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they looked up "automat" and it's a submachine-gun. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the question has not been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat your question, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That large Thompson, it was an unwieldy weapon. You said that it could have the charger with the 50 bullets. Is it closer to a German Schmeisser or a Russian Kalashnikov? What type would it be closer to?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't said that the charger could be -- could contain 50 rounds, but it's possible. I'm not a technical expert. Whether it's close to the Schmeisser or Kalashnikov, I would say it's closer to the Kalashnikov, but that's maybe a matter of interpretation. I come from tanks, we didn't have these kind of things. I mean I'm not an infantry soldier. We had bigger guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, it's not a question of interpretation, it's a question of professional knowledge. Since I'm a much better military expert than you, it is closer to a Schmeisser, because the Schmeisser and the Thompson use a pistol ammunition, whereas the Kalashnikov uses rifle ammunition, and that's why the Kalashnikov is an automatic rifle, whereas the Thompson and Schmeisser and Spagin and the M-56, they are submachine-guns, automatic. They're a little better than an automatic pistol, for example, as a weapon. So they're bigger than an automatic pistol and their charger is bigger, magazine clip, charger. So there's a difference between a submachine-gun and an automatic rifle, but if you don't know that, what can we do? But we'll continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have to stop. It's five past 10. I believe that in total you have 30 minutes left, Mr. Seselj. I'll make sure your time does not go over. Twenty-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed the hearing. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I promised to report back on the issue of Vasiljevic's various interviews and so on. Now, first I'd like to correct one thing. I think I sort of conceded that maybe the accused had not received private session or closed session parts of Vasiljevic's testimony in the Milosevic case. That's actually incorrect. By receipt, number 55 from the 6th of June, 2007, the accused was provided private session parts of Vasiljevic's testimony in the Milosevic case. I can distribute the receipts here, but I don't know if there's any need to, but I can do it if you'd like. The second issue is with respect to the suspect interview. We would be in a position to disclose -- or we will disclose a transcript that has been made of the recording of the suspect interview. We will give that to the accused as soon as we can get it printed and sent to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to see that certificate. Probably what Mr. Marcussen says is true, but I want to see it. I want to see the receipt right now, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It will be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is a receipt of the printed version, so it doesn't have the signature, but I'm getting the signature brought. It's coming in a little bit. Actually, I do have it here in a signed version. And I will refer the accused to items 40 and 41 on the second page of the table that is attached to the receipt.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it doesn't say here at all that I received those transcripts. It only says that the OTP conducted a search of all transcripts of closed and private sessions in order to find instances of the witness mentioning my name, and to hand over to me a list of those instances. It says: "We searched the transcripts and prepared the enclosed list with the name or pseudonym of the witness and the page number where your name is mentioned.
