The list covers the transcripts up to the 31st of August, 2006, and it was sent to Mr. Cooper on the 14th of September, 2006." "We are updating the search. We would be grateful if you were to confirm the receipt by signing the [indiscernible] list and returning it to our office." I received only this list, not the transcripts. That's evident from the receipt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, apparently it's a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It was my understanding that the transcripts had followed the receipt, but if the accused says he didn't receive them, then that might -- I stand corrected on that. What this list would do, though, would be to enable the accused to make the request to the Trial Chamber, and I did not intentionally mean to mislead the accused or the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let's complete the cross-examination. You have 25 minutes left, exactly. But before I give the floor to Mr. Seselj, I have a question. We were talking about Thompson guns, machine-guns, but I was still thinking of paramilitary units. To your knowledge, were paramilitary units that were in the field -- did they wear specific uniforms, did they have specific equipment, or was it very difficult to distinguish a paramilitary unit from a TO unit or a JNA unit? Were there, according to you, differences between the two? And to sum up my question, did the SRS volunteers bear specific signs that showed or suggested that they were members of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the various volunteers/paramilitary groups all had -- or many of them had their own badges and insignia, but they were not systematically worn on the battlefield. It seems that these badges and insignia were most often available in shops in Belgrade, and then people would buy them for whatever purpose. Now, to answer to your question, the easiest way to identify volunteers on the battlefield would be to look at their general aspect, in the sense that, for example, Seselj volunteers often wore long beards. Why? Because they wanted to look like some of the Chetniks who participated in earlier conflicts. Some of them had high hats, fur hats with the so-called cockade, so a metal insignia on it, but not all of them. Some of the volunteers were wearing a mixture of TO uniforms, so the so-called SMB, olive-drab, one-colour uniform, but mixed up with bits of stuff they would find somewhere else. The only paramilitary group that looked kind of dressed in a uniform way were the Arkan -- Arkan Serbian Volunteer Guard, where at least during parades they would be dressed in black overalls, and while participating in the conflict they would wear camouflage uniforms. There were also volunteers who had camouflage uniforms, but some of them would then be camouflage uniforms as those adopted by the JNA, for example, the Guards Motorised Brigade at one time in Vukovar received camouflage uniforms, or at least some members, but sometimes it was bits of uniforms they had found somewhere else. There's 65 ter number 2164 is a "Velika Serbia" article, and on the cover of the magazine where the article is taken from, one can see a picture of Mr. Seselj posing in uniform among other individuals in uniform, and from the contents of "Velika Serbia," one could draw the conclusion or one can -- one draws the conclusion that these people who are surrounding Mr. Seselj in uniform are all SRS volunteers. And this picture would show you actually the wide array of different natures of uniform and insignia that are worn even within one particular volunteer or paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, can you say what the percentage of volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party was that wore beards?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot say that, but some of the Vojvodas, for example, Slavko Aleksic was known for his beard, and I think in the documents Mr. Seselj handed over, there is a military booklet for Vaske, Vasilije Vidovic, and the picture, quite surprisingly, in the military booklet, you can basically see the face of Mr. Vidovic, but you see most of all the long beard. Now, I don't claim that all SRS volunteers wore beards, but at least some of them did. In particular -- I think this is particularly relevant because it was not common for members of the military to wear such long beards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the OTP has all the photographs of all the Chetnik Vojvodas I proclaimed. Do more of them have a beard or do most of them do not have a beard? This is ridiculous that he should identify volunteers of the SRS by their beards. That's the first time in my life I've heard of such a thing, but let him say so. Do more of them have beards or are more of them clean-shaven?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe something went wrong or I mis-expressed myself, but I didn't claim that every volunteer with a beard was an SRS volunteer. What I tried to say is that a number of significant or prominent SRS volunteers had long beards, which was unusual for people who are participating in armed conflicts as members of the armed forces. And two of them are Aleksic and Vaske, on the pictures I have seen, to be completely complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I want to say to you, Mr. Theunens, that you are unable to recognise a volunteer of the SRS by his external appearance and tell him apart from other volunteers and soldiers. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that respect, did you review JNA regulations about the fact of having a beard? Was it authorised or was it prohibited, to have a beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not familiar with the specific prescriptions in the JNA dealing with beards. Now, I know that from a military point of view, beards are considered a security risk because they make it more difficult to wear a gas mask. Now, I know from the members of the Guards Motorised Brigade in Vukovar that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the French Foreign Legions, you have bearded servicemen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, the engineers of the French Foreign Legion, it's part of their tradition, they have long beards, but I'm not sure whether they're allowed to carry these beards when they're sent to operations, in particular operations where there is a threat of the use of nuclear, biological, or chemical weapons. Now, to come back to the Guards Motorised Brigade, I was told by members of the Guards Motorised Brigade that at one moment in Vukovar, they decided not to shave anymore, but they never had beards like the two individuals I mentioned earlier, Aleksic and Vaske.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, the OTP has spent a vast amount of money to have translated all the JNA regulations and all the provisions, and you did not have time to read that and find the regulation prohibiting beards in the JNA to active duty officers and conscripts doing their military service, but reservists were allowed to have beards. You were unable to find this anywhere because you didn't read all the documents. A reservist, when called up into the reserves, could wear a beard. Of course, he had to be tidy. His beard was not permitted to be full of fleas. He would have to wash it regularly, but he could wear it. You didn't read this, and now, in your view, a beard is the main characteristic of volunteers of the SRS. But you didn't answer my question. Am I right when I say that judging by external appearances, you couldn't distinguish a volunteer of the SRS from other volunteers, territorials, JNA soldiers, and so on and so forth, judging by external appearance?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to emphasise that I never claimed that all volunteers wearing beards were SRS volunteers or that long beards were the main characteristics of volunteers of the SRS. Now, answering the second part of Mr. Seselj's question, by the -- as I said in the earlier question, the question of the Presiding Judge, from the overall looks, one could make a distinction between the JNA, TO and volunteers. Within the volunteers, it was more difficult to make a distinction because of the mixture of uniforms, but a number of SRS volunteers would wear particular insignia, like, for example, the "kokarda," or they would have a fur hat, or they would have a long beard, or any other characteristic which would assist in determining that these volunteers belonged to or -- belonged to an SRS volunteer detachment. But it's not the only criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of what? Just give me a single indication on the basis of which you could be sure that you were dealing with a volunteer of the SRS. Just say one thing. Did other volunteers wear cockades? Did regular soldiers take off their five-pointed stars and put cockades? In some places, the officers objected and other places they didn't. Why would a fur hat be a characteristic of the SRS when it belongs to the tradition of the entire Serbian people, or the Sajkaca cap? Just give me a single feature on the basis of which you could be sure, judging by external appearances, that a man was a volunteer of the SRS. It can't be a beard, it can't be a cockade. The cockades were being sold in the street; anyone could buy them. It can't be a uniform. So what can it be?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've tried to explain not only the complexity of the whole issue but also the fact that one would have to look at various characteristics. It is correct that seeing one individual in an isolated environment with a kokarda does not allow to conclude, well, this has to be an SRS volunteer. They have to have more factors. In whose company is this person? Where is this person active? What is this person doing? What is this person claiming, himself? Are there other volunteers? And this then, looking at these various aspects, would allow to conclude, yes, indeed we are dealing with a member of an SRS volunteer detachment. But seeing an isolated individual, I would agree with Mr. Seselj, it would be difficult or impossible to determine which volunteer group this individual determined -- belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you couldn't judge that by the company he kept, either. For example, in Leva Supoderica, there were locals, there were volunteers of the SRS, and there were also other volunteers, and you see them all together. How could you tell which of them was a volunteer of the SRS, which of them was some other kind of volunteer, and which of them was a territorial? Could they be told apart?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we're talking about Leva Supoderica, Leva Supoderica has been identified in SRS documentation, both documents from the war staff as well as "Velika Serbia" articles, as a Chetnik volunteer detachment. Now, this means that there are particular links between Leva Supoderica and the SRS. There is also a document indicating that the -- that the commander, Milan Lancuzanin was appointed through the intervention of the SRS war staff, which means, in my view, that Leva Supoderica, as I said, is an SRS volunteer detachment, including its members. Now, whether they consider themselves also TO, that is then of less relevance in the context of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How can you claim that the Serbian Radical Party appointed Lancuzanin commander of Leva Supoderica when that detachment of the Territorial Defence existed in Vukovar before the arrival of the Guards Brigade and our volunteers, and when Lancuzanin had nothing to do with the Serbian Radical Party? In late October or early November 1991, that's when he joined the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj is providing here an additional piece of information. This detachment, Leva Supoderica Detachment, according to what Mr. Seselj told us, it existed before the arrival of the SRS volunteers. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm checking my report. I think it would be helpful when we -- there is an article by Branislav Vakic which is actually P55, when Branislav Vakic talks about his experiences in Vukovar as well as other combat areas, and this is on page -- English page 117 of part 2 of my report, where Vakic states, among other things: "One group of Chetniks had already been deployed on the approaches to town under the command of Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni," and so on. And he refers there to the 1st of November 1991. So I stand corrected for the appointment of Lancuzanin, but at least Lancuzanin is confirmed by the Radical Party as the person in command of the Leva Supoderica Chetnik Volunteer Detachment. And the reference to the Chetnik Volunteer Detachment is made in, for example, in the order proclaiming Lancuzanin to Chetnik Vojvoda, which is the order number 124, 65 ter number 1841.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the fact that these people refer to themselves as Chetniks even before the arrival of the Guards Brigade doesn't link them to the Serbian Radical Party, does it, because the Serbian Radical Party cannot have a monopoly on all Chetniks, can it? We discussed this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but if we have people who refer to themselves as Chetniks who are member of a unit which is identified in several documents by the Serbian Radical Party as a Chetnik volunteer detachment, we can conclude from that that the use of the term "Chetnik" by these people to identify themselves is accepted and agreed with by the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, you're a very clever man, and you always answer in line with the case you develop in your report, but the question went much deeper than your answer. The question of the accused was whether before the arrival of the SRS volunteers, whether there was not a unit that had called itself "Chetnik," without there being any link whatsoever with the SRS. Then you should have answered "yes" or "no," but that's not the way you answered. You added something else in order to bring back the question within the remit of your own case. So I'm going to ask you the question, and then you'll answer by "yes" or "no." And the question is the following: Before SRS volunteers arrived in the Vukovar region, was there already a detachment of local people, a detachment that had self-proclaimed itself or called itself "Chetnik"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot answer the question, because I have not been able to establish the circumstances how Leva Supoderica was founded and so on and so on. From the documents, including my report, the answer would be -- I'm just trying to read the question again. The answer would be "yes," but, again, I don't think it's a conclusive answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, now listen to me carefully, and please don't respond to something that is not contained in my question. How did volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, in the Serbian villages of Slavonia, from April to September 1991, obtain weapons? Where did they get weapons from? Answer me that.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that question was already asked before the break, and I replied that they received the weapons from -- in the area, so from the local village defence. However, while reviewing my report during the break, I also found a statement by Mr. Soskocanin, who participated in the incident in Borovo Selo, who made a reference to the JNA. It's a very general reference, but, anyway, that's included in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, they could not have obtained the weapons from the local Territorial Defence because long before this, the JNA took all the weapons from the Territorial Defence in all the federal units of the former Yugoslavia, and you are aware of this, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am aware of the order of May 1990 by General Adzic to relocate the weapons of the TO's, of the Republic's, and the autonomous provinces, to JNA warehouses, but I also understood that some of these weapons in the course -- I mean, already before [Realtime transcript read in error "throughout"] the conflict were redistributed to Serbs in various parts of Croatia. I have not dealt with that aspect in detail in my report. Just for the transcript, I said "before the conflict," so already starting somewhere in 1990, 1991. There is information that the JNA assisted in -- together with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia and the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia, in redistribute weapons to Serbs in various parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If the JNA supplied those weapons, and we saw what those weapons were like, they were obsolete, Thompsons, Russian Spagin, M-48 rifles, M-56 submachine-guns, do you know of a single JNA unit which used such weapons in the time period we are talking about, a single one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Mr. Seselj said, Your Honours, these were obsolete weapons, and I understand they were still stored in JNA depots, but I have no information that they were still in use by JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To cut this short, I'll tell you what I know about this, and you can confirm whether it's correct or not. These are weapons written off by the JNA, set aside to be destroyed. General Dusan Pekic, one of the functionaries of the Association of Serbs from Croatia, using his private contacts and channels, because he was a well-known, famous commander from World War II, one of the most able generals the JNA ever had, and although he had been a partisan, I speak very highly of him, so he had good contacts. And using his private contacts with certain officers, he managed to obtain those weapons which had been earmarked for destruction. Am I correct in saying this? You mentioned Dusan Pekic in your report.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, in general terms I'm familiar with that, but I would just like to refer also to my report, English page 40 of part 2, where Mr. Seselj himself makes a number of statements on the weaponry of SRS/SCP volunteers. In 65 ter number 750, he talks about the fact that SRS volunteers since recently possess the most modern weapons, and this is a statement he makes in November 1991. In November 1993, Mr. Seselj states that weapons were received from the army and the police. So just to complete the answer given by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what do you care what I said in 1993, Mr. Theunens? What sort of evidence is that, something I said in a speech or an interview in 1993? What kind of evidence do you consider that to be, as an expert?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider all the public statements by -- in the context of this report, I consider the public statements made by Mr. Seselj of relevance. It's certainly material I would consider. And then applying the methodology I explained earlier, I would look for corroboration and then see whether the information included in the statement by Mr. Seselj is corroborated by other sources. And if it is, I would include it in my report, independent of the time period Mr. Seselj made the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on, Mr. Seselj, we have been given a document in B/C/S by the Registrar, Mr. Seselj. I don't know what the contents of this document is, but let me just draw your attention to the fact that apparently this document relates to a protected witness, as of today. Therefore, if you intend to use this document, we'll need to move into private session to deal with this particular document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, I'll tell you what this document is about, which I just received by fax from Belgrade, from my legal advisers, when we finish the examination of this witness. It concerns another issue, but it's my duty to inform you of it today. It's a problem that has newly arisen, but it has nothing to do with the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, have you found certain contradictions in the statements I made in various periods of time? For example, in 1991, at a press conference, I stated that we obtained these obsolete weapons from Hungary and that a Hungarian minister was involved in the shipment. In 1993, I attacked Milosevic and his police, saying they had given this to us. Do I have the right, as a politician, to launch smoke screens in certain situations for a certain purpose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This cannot be answered by the witness. He's a military expert. Whatever his opinion about what would be legitimate political statements by the accused is irrelevant. Whether -- the first part, whether the witness had noticed any discrepancies in the accused's statements that are the basis for his report, now, that might be a fair question, but these things about what he, as a politician, is allowed to say is -- has nothing to do with the expertise of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. President, I am a politician at all times, even when here in the courtroom. I remain a politician and active on the Serbian political scene, extremely active. As a politician in 1991 and 1993, I spoke about the sources of arming the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party. In 1991, I accused the Hungarian minister. In 1993, I accused Milosevic, now, with the exclusive aim of protecting the real source of the weaponry, and that's the essence of my question. And now I come to a new question, another question, after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we are all here to discover the truth, you are saying that in 1991, you made statements. This was to protect the real source. I assume that you're also in favour of the truth. All the more reason to put a question to the witness and say, "In 1991, I said such-and-such, but the purpose of this was such-and-such. If I'm telling you this now, the arms came through this channel, do you agree with me?" And like that, we can move forward.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness confirmed it when I mentioned General Pekic a moment ago, but then he happened to remember my statement in 1993, which I made when I was in this terrible clash with Milosevic, when Milosevic was arresting volunteers en masse, so I used everything at my disposal, any means that I had, to hit Milosevic, defending my own people. I would lay down my life for them, let alone make smoke screens in public, set up smoke screens in public. However, my next question:

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the police have depots, warehouses, with so many weapons in the first place, and did the police have this type of weapon: The Thompson, the Spagin-type weapon, the M-56, the M-48? You, as a military expert, must have known of at least one police depot with weapons like that if the police indeed had something like that. To cut a long story short, we see that it's impossible that the police had these weapons, and if it didn't have the weapons, it couldn't have provided them and supplied the volunteers. General Pekic supplied us with those weapons because, through secret channels, he managed to come by those weapons before they were destroyed. That's my thesis. You mentioned General Pekic and you know that he had a role in sending the volunteers out and in equipping them, so that's the essence of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you confirm or deny that the arms were given to the volunteers through the channel of General Pekic, who was able, through his networks, to send arms who seemingly were designed for destruction? Can you confirm Mr. Seselj's theory or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I confirm that thesis, but it's not the only channel. I am aware that in -- I'm not sure if it was 1989 or 1990, that, for example -- that in Serbia, weapons of the civil defence and also weapons that were used or could be used in time of conflict or other condition when there was a requirement to do so, to protect factories and so on, were all confiscated or brought together, and I'm not sure anymore whether that was done by the Ministry of Defence or the Ministry of Interior. Just to come back to Pekic, I think in any organised country, and the SFRY was certainly an organised country in 1990, you cannot just redistribute weapons through private channel -- channels. Procedures have to be followed, documents have to be established, and so on and so on. So the police most likely didn't have any Thompsons or M-84's or other old weapons in its equipment, but one cannot rule out that the police or the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Serbia played a role in organising the transit or redistribution of these weapons, and that's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're now guessing. That's guesswork. You haven't got a shred of evidence that up to September 1991, that the Ministry of Defence, that the JNA or the Serbian police from Serbia took part in any of that. You mentioned 1990. Now, in 1990, Yugoslavia still looked like a well-ordered state. Now, in 1991, there was chaos and people were leaving the JNA, Croatian generals were leaving the JNA day by day. We would just hear one person left, the other person left, one taking a whole truckload of documents, the other one taking goodness knows what else. So the JNA was undergoing a situation of chaos. And in that chaos, it is possible that General Pekic told a colonel over there who was in charge of destroying old weapons, out-of-date weapons that were dangerous to the person using them, because what would happen would be that the barrel of a Thompson would explode and could injure the man shooting, so he could tell the man, "Don't destroy that. Draw up a record and say that you destroyed it, but I'm going to drive in a truck and take the weapons away." Is that possible, Mr. Theunens, in 1991, with all the chaos that went on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without speculating, because there has perhaps been some speculation here. It seems that in 1991, the situation was chaotic. The Croatian officers and generals are leaving their positions, seemingly the JNA is no longer commanded by anyone, and General Pekic then intervenes and may have asked those people who were keeping these weapons to hand them out. Is that a possibility or not, given all the information you were able to gather, or can't you say anything about this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I stand on my previous answer. I mean, the answer I gave to the previous question, there was chaos in certain areas and on certain levels, but I do not think, based on the documentation I reviewed and the information I have consulted, that this is sufficient to explain the arming of Serbs in certain areas of Croatia, in particular looking at the scale of these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So where did the weapons come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have seen evidence indeed that weapons came from depots, JNA depots, where these obsolete or outdated weapons were being stored. I've also seen information that weapons that had been put -- TO weapons that had been put under JNA control in 1990, May 1990, were then redistributed. I've also seen information, the example I mentioned with the submachine-guns or machine-guns - I've forgot exactly which type it was - that were used in Serbia by I'm not sure whether it was civil defence or whether they were part of defence structures that should protect factories and other facilities of importance, that these weapons were collected at one moment in time with the intervention of the Ministry of Defence and the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, and that weapons of that type were then later found among Serbs in Croatia, as these were, for example, Thompsons and M-84.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did the Ministry of Defence of Serbia and the Ministry of the Interior collect those weapons? What year was that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I indicated, I'm not sure of the year. I think I recall it's 1989 or 1990. I remember this information and a lot of things from -- I think those were statements made at -- at one moment in time by Vice-Admiral Jokic who was around that time period or in 1991, during a certain time period in 1991, Minister of Defence of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, if the Ministry of Defence of Serbia and the MUP of Serbia, in 1989 and 1990, and in 1989 the Ministry of the Defence of Serbia didn't exist at all, as far as I remember, it was only in 1990 that it came into existence, but if they gathered up the weapons then, then I assume they sent it out to JNA warehouses straightaway; isn't that right? The moment they handed them over to the JNA, all their links to those weapons ceased. The JNA collected up all the Territorial Defence weapons so that it could keep it under its control, because you can feel tension in the air and the possible abuse or misuse of those weapons, and there was the first conflict between the JNA and the Croatian leadership at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There is no question being put. There's just a statement without a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, is what I'm telling you right, is it correct? There, you have a question. Is what I've just said correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it doesn't correspond with my recollection, and I would just like to correct that indeed in 1989, we don't have a Ministry of Defence, we have a Secretariat for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'd just like to let you know that you have five minutes left, and at 11.15, that will be it, as far as you are concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll complete within that time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you know that some other pensioned-off generals of the JNA, together with Dusan Pekic, took part in collecting up obsolete, written-off JNA weapons for the Serb villages in Slavonia, Dalmatia and in other places? For example, General Radojica Nenezic, have you heard of him? He was born in Slavonia. Pekic is from Kordun. They are all generals who were born in the area of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the name of the second general, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In greater -- in "Velika Serbia," did you see that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party from Borovo Selo, who were victorious over the hundreds of policemen on the 2nd of May, Croatian policemen on the 2nd of May, Djuric promoted them and gave them certain ranks. And I assume the Prosecutor provided you with that article that appeared in "Velika Serbia"; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not a matter that I include information provided by the Prosecutor in my report. I selected all the documents and all the information included in my report myself, without any intervention of the Prosecutor, except for that, okay, I work in the Office of the Prosecutor and I have to consult the databases of the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, I am familiar with that information, and this is actually included in page 104, part 2 of the English version of the report, and it's based on 65 ter number 320. That is the "Velika Serbia" article entitled: "When a Serbian trumpet sounds in Borovo Selo."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that at the end of August, the leadership of the Serbian Radical Party, and I personally, had several talks with high-ranking officers of the JNA, generals, colonels, captains of naval vessels, about sending volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party to the JNA, and after that Ljubisa Petkovic sent out instructions according to which all the volunteers should return from the Slavonian villages in order to regroup? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the specific talks, but I'm aware of the fact that there were contacts between officials of the Serbian Radical Party and certain high-ranking JNA officers, but I'm not sure that this was only in 1991 or also in 1992, and even when the JNA transformed into the VJ, and some names are included in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps this will be my last question, so please listen to me carefully. Is it true and correct that as of September 1991, until the 19th of May, 1992, the Serbian Radical Party did not send its volunteers anywhere outside the composition of the JNA, outside any cooperation with the JNA? Do you agree with that, from September 1991 to the 19th of May, 1992? The 19th of May, 1992, is the date of the ultimatum for the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the -- the question sounds very simple, but the answer is more complicated, because in Western Slavonia, when we're discussing the events in Vocin, and I mentioned earlier the letter by General Talic, when he's asked to provide information on the events in Vocin in December 1991, and I'm talking now about 65 ter number 1037, Talic says that the SRS volunteers -- or that the forces of the TO in Slavonia, in the villages of Hum and Vocin near Podravska Slatina, were in that area. We have established in the report the links between those local Serb TO units and SRS volunteers. And Talic says, "Well, look, they were not in the composition of the 5th Corps." Now, for what Vukovar is concerned, there the answer is "yes" without any doubt. Now, for what Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, we know from the documents that in Bosanski Samac, the answer is "yes." For other areas like, for example, Zvornik, the documents of the 17 Corps suggest that there is no direct involvement of the 17 Corps in the -- in the events, including the participation of SRS-affiliated volunteers. Whether this has been agreed upon on a higher level of the JNA, I have not been able to establish, but the fact that these volunteers are able to be deployed, and as we saw at Boskoski Samac, that they can use helicopters and so on to be sent, indeed shows that there is cooperation and agreement on the highest level within the JNA for these SRS volunteers to be sent to these areas during that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Two very short questions. When was it that Talic gave the statement you just quoted, what year?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 29 -- this is a letter he sends on the 29th of March, 1992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do the papers tell you that the entire Territorial Defence of Western Slavonia including the volunteers, was on the salary list of the 5th Corps? Do the papers testify to that, and the commander of the entire Territorial Defence in Western Slavonia, was he an active colonel of the JNA by the name of Trbojevic? Is that correct? Do you know when the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were sent to take part in the operation to liberate Zvornik, that the Bubanj Potok barracks in Belgrade, the JNA barracks, they went there and took over the uniforms and weapons from there, and from there they went to Zvornik, escorted by a police escort, they didn't go by bus or by bike like you? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are four questions in this particular passage of the accused's purported questioning of the witness. Now, if the accused wants the witness to answer this question, I think he should be allowed at least the time to deal with each one of the four, or the accused should reformulate this question if he still has time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the problem is that this witness would need 40 minutes to answer these four questions, that's the problem, whereas you have restricted my time. So what can I do about that? You know, sometimes I can ask rhetorical questions that I don't expect an answer to, because my questions in themselves are very convincing and illustrate my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are four sub-questions, so the question is a lengthy one. Can you answer this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I will be -- I will try to be as short as possible. Trbojevic, the answer is "yes." Zvornik, the answer is "yes." For the payment, the answer is very short, I do not know, because from the documents of the war staff, one can see that SRS volunteers are also being paid in Belgrade through the SRS war staff. I don't say "by" but through the assistance of the SRS war staff. So it could well be that a number of volunteers were on the pay list of the 5th Corps, but we also have these documents. And the fourth question, I forgot. I mean, I don't see it on the transcript anymore, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I have any more time, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your time is up. You have had five hours, but if you have one last question which you were unable to put to the witness and which is very important, then just put it to the witness and we'll stop after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know the structure of the war staff of the Serbian Radical Party. Well, you're well acquainted with it, and you know who compiled it. And in the examination-in-chief, we were instructed not to mention names, so I'm not going to do so. Now, this war staff, according to its structure, could it have been at all an organ of command in any way, command of military actions, operations, tactical attacks, defence operations and so on? Was it capacitated and professional enough to do that or was it a war staff which could only rally volunteers, take them to the barracks so that they could put on uniforms, and take weapons, to keep records of who they are, to see to the funerals of those killed, to see to paying out financial assistance to the families of killed volunteers, to send the sick and wounded for treatment, and so on and so forth? It's a long question, but it's simple in essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you reply, this is a question I've put already, but please answer it nonetheless, because it's an important question and it could very well conclude the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not come across information indicating that the SRS war staff gets involved in strictly operational matters and is commanding military activity or actions and operations from Belgrade. However, I have tried to show in the report that the activities of the SRS war staff go beyond what Mr. Seselj has stated in his question and also include the issuing of instructions to volunteers, no matter how general these volunteers -- these instructions are, and that the war staff also keeps information on the way how the volunteers carried out their duties or their activities, including disciplinary matters, and as such is in a position to act against volunteers -- SRS volunteers who have violated certain disciplinary provisions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more short question. Just three seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which sanctions could the war staff proclaim if a volunteer was undisciplined to punish them? Was the only sanction to exclude them from the Serbian Radical Party so that that volunteer could no longer be sent to the front anywhere? Was that the only sanction that the war staff could take for lack of discipline on a soldier's part, a volunteer's part?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- this is not the only sanction, because like any citizen who becomes aware of the fact that -- or the information that somebody -- that another citizen has committed a crime which could be -- could amount to a -- excuse me, I will rephrase that, that any other citizen has committed an act which could amount to a crime, well, I think in any country you have the duty to inform the competent authorities, who would then do their job. I don't claim in the report that it was up to the SRS war staff to put people in prison, but at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall rephrase this question. Have you seen any documents of the Serbian Radical Party stating that it would have been informed of crimes through reports that would have been forwarded to the SRS? Was the party informed of the existence of crimes committed by members of the Serbian Radical Party? Have you seen any report to that effect, i.e., that would have been notified to the war staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have only seen documents where the war staff is notified of -- of lack of discipline, including a document which is 65 ter 657, where the war staff sends a letter to the commander of Leva Supoderica to inform them in writing about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I was about to call you "Commander." You know full well what the difference is in the army between disciplinary matters which come under military discipline and crimes that are committed. That is another story. When you say that crimes are committed, are you talking about a breach in matters of discipline? Was the war staff entitled to deal with disciplinary issues or was it only a political body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in 65 ter number 657, it is the war staff -- I mean, the chief of the war staff himself who asks the commander of Leva Supoderica, on the 9th of November, 1991, to inform "us," i.e., the war staff in writing "about the soldiers that you have sent back due to lack of discipline or any other reason, as well as about the soldiers who have shown exceptional bravery." It is clear that there is a difference between violations of discipline and crimes, but they are related to each other if -- or my conclusion is that if the war staff asks to be informed about disciplinary issues, it would not -- it would be logical that they would also ask to be informed about crimes, because when a disciplinary issue has been observed, it's not clear whether this amounts to a crime or not from the very beginning, and so there has to be an investigation. So my conclusion is, well, if the war staff asks to know about disciplinary issues, it would make sense they would also want to know about criminal issues. For the disciplinary matters, as Mr. Seselj says, it appears that the only sanction is to remove that volunteer from the SRS and prevent him from going to the battlefield again as an SRS volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor to Mr. Marcussen, because I'm looking at the clock and there is a redirect, and my colleague would also like to put questions. You are saying that you had this document which indicates that the war staff is asking to be informed of any breach of discipline, but the question I've asked you is this: Are there any documents that inform the war staff of the existence of crimes? I do stress the words "existence of crimes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not seen such a document addressed to the SRS war staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That was my question. The Prosecution now has the floor for its redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think I can be brief, so I hope we can finish today. For Your Honours' information, I'm going to concentrate on one matter that came up yesterday and today, and it relates to the issue of Vojvoda and the precise -- well, the implications of the appointments of Vojvoda. And I would be showing Your Honours two videos -- two clips that I'd ask the expert to comment on. The first clip is 65 ter number 1836, and we will be showing it here in Sanction, the programme we use to show these sort of things. It's a clip which lasts about four minutes. It is from Serbian Television in Bosnia. It is from the 15th of May, 1993, and it relates to the order number 124 where -- which proclaims a number of people Vojvodas. So that is the 65 ter number 1841. So that is the actual order that we have been discussing, and the video clip number, I should maybe also indicate the ERN number for it, it is V000-0278, and it is clip C. And maybe we could show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] New Serbian Chetnik Vojvodas. Order number 124. As the only Chetnik Vojvoda directly engaged in the present day struggle for the liberation of the Serbian people following the tradition of the Serbian people and the Serbian Chetniks for exceptional achievements in the war, great heroism and proven skills in warfare of the most distinguished of the commanders, I hereby pronounce the oath of the 18 new Vojvodas was something that Romanija Mountain was very happy about. It is an oath it has not heard for 50 years. I swear, as the Serbian Chetnik Vojvoda, I swear to God and St. Sava -- I swear by God and St. Sava that I will fight with all my might for the freedom of the Serbian people, that I will fight with all my might for the freedom of the Serbian people and the restoration of a unified Serbian state in the Balkans which will encompass all Serbian lands, and the restoration of a unified Serbian state in the Balkans which will encompass all Serbian lands, so help me God, so help me God. Amen, Amen. Good luck and bless you. May God give you a long life. One can trust them, that that's how it's going to be. The rank of Chetnik Vojvoda was bestowed on the following Serbian heroes from all Serbian areas: Zdravko Abramovic, Slavko Aleksic, Mirko Blagojevic, Branislav Vakic, Nedejlko Vidakovic, Miroslav Vukovic, Cele, Branislav Gavrilovic-Brne, Milika Dacevic, Ceko, Zoran Drazilovic, Cica, Todor Lazic, Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, Mitar Maksimovic, Manda, Tomislav Nikolic, Jovo Ostojic, Ljubisa Petkovic and Srecko Radovanovic. Brne, Brne, turn around just a little bit so I can capture you a bit. Ah, that's good. Is that Crna? Then Sokolac, a monument city to Serbhood where Vojvoda Seselj spoke to the people in his capacity as the president of the Serbian Radical Party. If it comes to a foreign intervention, thousands upon thousands of our volunteers will cross the River Drina and come to you, all of us whom you see here today will be with you here and we will share your fate. After the rally, Mr. Seselj, accompanied by the newly-appointed Vojvodas, headed to Pale to a meeting with Dr. Radovan Karadzic, the president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, have you seen this video before?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, Your Honours, and I included the transcript in my report. It's 65 ter number 6062. It's in part 2 on page 78.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what conclusions did you draw from this and other documentation you have seen with respect to the status of Vojvoda?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, we went over this during the previous days, but I conclude that Vojvodas are people with authority among the volunteers. Even if they had command positions in SRS detachments prior to being appointed or proclaimed Vojvoda, the fact that they are proclaimed Vojvoda shows that Mr. Seselj wants to confirm their authority and, as such, their prestige among the volunteers. Something I forgot to mention yesterday but is included in my report is on the English page 85 in part 2 of the report, where the Federal Minister of Defence, Pavle Bulatovic, so the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, on the 5th of July, 1993, when the matter of the appointment or the proclamation of Vojvodas is being discussed by the FRY Supreme Defence Council, Bulatovic states that: "The granting of Vojvoda titles by Seselj means that he must have an army. Otherwise, why would someone be dubbed a duke just for himself?" And so on and so on. I mean, this can be found on page 85.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, I would like the witness to look at another video. This is much shorter, Your Honours. It is from 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question, please. We've seen this video clip right now, and we note that there's a religious connotation in that ceremony, since we see the men cross themselves, and we see that furthermore there are two men in civilian clothes, whereas all the others are undoubtedly wearing military clothes. So we see that they are wearing military clothes, and I thought that these men were members of a military unit. So would you agree that the Vojvoda we see on these images belonged to a military unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, most of the uniforms I could recognise were uniforms of the VRS, so the armed force of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we could see, for example, Slavko Aleksic is one of the people -- one of the persons with the long beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do believe we will actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We will get to see more of Aleksic now. The next video is 65 ter number 6048. The ERN number is V000-1506, clip B. It is -- it's part of a recording that was done for a documentary called "Bloody Bosnia" by Maggie O'Kane, and according to the information I have, it's from the 7th of April, 1994. Let's have a look at the video, please. I should say that we don't have an English transcript of this video. We will provide that. It's a two-minute video. The language spoken on the video is English. We have provided the accused with the B/C/S translation of what is being said, and of course the interpreters have that transcript too. So let's look at the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, is this a video you have seen before today?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I haven't seen this video before, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Does that in any way change your analysis of the meaning of "Vojvoda"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, and it also shows an interesting perspective of the nature of the volunteers, or motivation, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is an impermissible manner of continuing the examination-in-chief. This is not redirect. I'm very happy to have seen this video for the first time in my life, and I'm very proud of it - please don't misunderstand me - but I think the Prosecutor's behaviour is impermissible. He's continuing his examination-in-chief, instead of attempting to rehabilitate his witness where he stumbled in cross-examination. Instead, he's simply continuing his examination-in-chief, and it's simply impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Redirect must be in relation to the direct examination, and the direct examination concerned -- included a number of questions related to Vojvodas. So this can be completed, Mr. Marcussen. However, the last video clip, I saw the image of a man dressed in black. What are those clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It didn't look like official uniform. I saw a religious connotation in it, because the individual was also wearing a cross. And I know that members of the Orthodox church, I mean clergymen, wear a black dress. I cannot say any more about it. We also saw a person in civilian attire, with a civilian hat, and he had a cockade on the hat. So it shows the nature of some of the volunteers we are dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it goes very fast on these videos, and I appreciate that. I just wanted to clarify what is being said on the video is that this is a volunteer that had come from New York, he had been there the summer before, participated in the fighting, and he has come back. So I think when you review the video, it will be clear, that he's a volunteer and so he would seem to be one of the people under Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, there was also a gentleman in a uniform, sporting a beard. Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've seen Slavko Aleksic, and I'm not sure about the other individual in uniform. I think there was one other or two other individuals in uniform, but I cannot recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I request -- I respectfully request the admission of these two videos, so that would be the admission of V000-0278, clip C, and V000-1506, clip B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two numbers, Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They will be Exhibit number P255, and clip B will be Exhibit number P256.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this completes my re-examination --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I should not be cut off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, I have an objection, and I do have the right to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. I'll give you the floor for your objection, but I would like Mr. Marcussen to finish before. What did you mean to say, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, sorry, if it's an objection to the admission of these documents -- these videos, then it's fine. I have two other matters that I need to address with the Court before I finish, but it's not necessary to have the witness for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what is your objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see Mr. Marcussen was nervous for no reason. My objection is to the second video. I demand that the OTP find the entire footage of this broadcast and disclose it to me, and also that the entire footage be admitted into evidence. I don't need this in the case of the first clip because I know exactly what it is, but as for the second clip, because there are journalists' comments on it, I want to see the entire footage. And when I see that, then I will be able to state my position on it. This was not an exhibit before, and you can see that the expert never saw it before, either. This is a guerrilla sort of way of introducing evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you knew about the existence of both these video clips for a long time, because they had been disclosed to you. You seem to be discovering these clips today, but I would strongly advise you to look closely to all the video clips that have been disclosed to you. If you had done so before, you could have asked the Prosecution to give you the entire programme, if there is a larger programme, I don't know, in order to possibly object. As you very well know, the decision made about admittance takes into account the issue of relevance, but in any case the weight will be determined at the end, based on all the evidence. So you will have an opportunity, with future witnesses, to oppose the content of this video or -- of this video clip or even when you hear your witnesses, to ask them questions about this guy who comes from New York and explains that he took part in the struggles. Mr. Marcussen, what were the issues you wanted to address?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first issue arises from an omission on my part. We have discussed and the witness testified about 65 ter number 1023. He -- it has actually been discussed a number of times, but he -- in particular, I asked him about it at transcript page 4029. As the debate went on, I forgot to request an exhibit number for this document. I would like to request an exhibit number for that. That's the first thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So it's document 1023, because I heard my interpreter say "1063". Is it 1023?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, give us a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, I demand that we see that document on the screen. I cannot remember documents by their number. If it was not admitted at the time it was mentioned, we have to see it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document 1023 is in binder --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It is in binder number 2, Your Honour, and I can read out the title. I'm sure the accused would recognise this, because he has, himself, been putting questions about it, I believe. It is -- well, the second page is: "Conclusions of the evaluation of the situation in the BiH territory in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Military District." And the things that were discussed from this document were basically arming of paramilitary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember that this document has been discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection. I simply wanted to see the document so I would know what document it was. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P257.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The second issue is unrelated to the evidence of the witness. I don't know whether you want to release the witness first, or I can go on as -- as Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said I wanted to discuss some administrative matters, and I did that before, so I should have precedence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, Mr. Marcussen, my first question is the following: Have you finished with your redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Harhoff has a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, having read your report and having heard you giving testimony here, I have a few questions relating to the war staff. First of all, it is unclear to me whether Mr. Seselj himself was a member of the SRS war staff. Can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. According to the documents included in my report -- I mean, the documents I include in my report do not include information on whether or not Mr. Seselj was a member of the war staff. Based on the documents, somebody else was in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So Mr. Seselj was never, himself, a direct member of the war staff; is that how we should understand what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I'm saying is that according to the documents, Mr. Seselj was not a member of the war staff. Now, whether he was a member outside the context of the documents, that's something I cannot establish, but I just want to clarify your very categoric conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Seselj took part in the war staff's meetings?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from the documents that deal with the dispatching of SRS volunteers that are discussed in the report, that they stated the detachment has been sent following the orders of the war staff and Mr. Seselj, but I cannot establish whether this means that Mr. Seselj was discussing the deployment directly with the war staff or how that decision was taken by Seselj -- Mr. Seselj and the war staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We spoke yesterday or the day before, I can't remember, about the issue of whether two gentlemen had been sent from Belgrade to lead the fight around Sarajevo. I think it was in Ilidza. And the Chamber ended by accepting that Mr. Seselj or the SRS had not sent these two gentlemen from Belgrade to Ilidza, but that these two gentlemen came from Sarajevo, themselves, and therefore joined the local SRS party organisation in Sarajevo, out of which they then took upon themselves to lead the armed fight in Ilidza. Now, my question in extension of that discussion we had yesterday is: What were the relations, in general, between the headquarters in Belgrade and the party organisations in -- where we had them, of course, in Bosnia and Herzegovina and also in Croatia? Can you explain to us a bit how the -- sort of the command structure or the communication structure was between the centre in Belgrade and the party organisations in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your permission, I would first like to address the issue of the two gentlemen who were -- whether they were sent by Belgrade or not, and I believe we were talking about Slavko Aleksic and Branislav Gavrilovic. I would like to make a slight correction to Branislav Gavrilovic, because we know that he was active in Croatia in 1991 and early 1992. And according to an article describing his activities, an article published in "Velika Serbia," and this is 65 ter 2164, Gavrilovic, according to this article, returns to Sarajevo based on the permission he has received from Mr. Seselj and the SRS war staff. So I think that's an important clarification we have to make for the first part. For the second part, I have not been able to establish the nature of the contacts between SRS chapters in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the SRS in Belgrade. I have included one document where the chief of the SRS war staff authorises Nikodin Cavic, who is the president of the SRS in Banja Luka, to gather volunteers, establishing in this letter Petkovic -- or, excuse me, the president of the SRS war staff also established a number of criteria that have to be applied before selecting volunteers. That is the furthest I can go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, but I would, nevertheless, seek to have some clarification. And let me do this by putting a question to you, and you can say "yes" or "no" if you know. Would, say, the local SRS party organisation in a particular area, in Sarajevo, Mostar, or Western Slavonia, would they be able, on their own, to recruit local men to form part of volunteers for the purpose of combat, or, and this is the alternative, or were volunteers only recruited from the SRS organisation in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter from the chief of the SRS war staff to Cavic indicates that a local -- or a chapter of the SRS in Bosnia-Herzegovina is authorised by Belgrade to recruit volunteers, and so they don't do it on their own initiative, according to this letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, if I may finish. So are you saying that if a local SRS party organisation somewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina actually recruited volunteers and trained them for combat, that would be done according to an authorisation from the SRS organisation in Belgrade; is that how we are to conclude?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, that is what the document says, and I can only say what the document says. Maybe there were other examples, but I am not aware of those, so I can only conclude or draw conclusions from that document, which is included in my report, but I don't know the 65 ter number by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to intervene, Judges, because the witness here is misleading you. He's mentioning a document dated 1991 in which Ljubisa Petkovic authorises Nikodin Cavic from Banja Luka to send volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party to Western Slavonia. Nikodin Cavic at the time was the initiator of the formation of the Serbian Radical Party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The party was still not registered in Bosnia-Herzegovina, however. And because of that, he was given instructions from Ljubisa Petkovic. In 1992, the party was registered in Republika Srpska --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's not for the accused to comment on this. He's testifying about the contents of the document. The document is on record. The time will come for him to lead evidence on this. This is not proper.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to prevent the Trial Chamber from being led astray, duped. The party, in 1992, was registered both in Republika Srpska and in the Republika Srpska Krajina. There were four Serbian radical parties: One in Serbia, an independent party; another in Montenegro; a third in Republika Srpska; a fourth in Republika Srpska Krajina. And they coordinated their work, but they were separate political parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, you will have ample opportunity to elicit this evidence from other witnesses. I don't think it makes any sense for you to testify at this moment. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Theunens, let me thank you, because we've just concluded your testimony. I'm going to let you go back to your customary work. And I'd like to ask the usher to walk you out of the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm aware we need to adjourn for the plenary, but I do have an issue or a few issues related to the scheduling for next week that I would like to draw to the Chamber's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution -- are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution provided you with two documents which were not used during the examination-in-chief and, therefore, were not admitted. Those two documents are very important ones. One is under number 1312. It is a document of the State Security Department in Belgrade on the 14th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would like to discuss these documents in private session. I know what the accused is referring to, but these documents are the subject of a request. I think -- I'm not sure whether Your Honours' ruling that has come out with respect to these particular documents is caught up by that, so I think we have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's move into private session, because this is a pending question. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we are in open session. We have come to the end of our hearing and shall resume our next hearing on Tuesday at a quarter past 2.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction "at a quarter to 3.00."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
